status: Proposed redraw for John’s review, 19 November 2026
art_method: Built-in ImageGen edit of the original camera still B. A second local image edit removed a stray third tip at the last crossing. Only that small patch was placed back into the full-size illustration.

reference_notes.B: June 8 camera clip 0022, 02:53. Across the two rows of seedlings, with John on the far side, his pale-green shed behind him and the number 7 shed to the right. This is the camera position and original outfit used.
reference_notes.C: Construction scale and height. John is raised on a chair in this frame, so the ground-standing figure in B is the scale reference.
reference_notes.D: Finished row. The long pale weathered canes look slender, with varying tapers, lengths above the crossings, minor single bows and some irregularity in the ridge. The lower green intermediates in the footage belong to a later step. This picture shows the main frame described on page 166.
reference_notes.E: Two distinct lines of feet alongside the existing bean plants, with the open soil strip between them.
reference_notes.F: Crossed bamboo tips and the ridge secured with short green plastic-coated wire. Hand-twisted ends point at different angles; the knot occupies a small fraction of the cane length.
reference_notes.A: Same shoot, facing the camera. Source for the fleece, brown shirt, open checked layer, microphone, sunlight and wire in hand.
reference_notes.FACE_FRONT: Frontal camera crop for John's jawline, chin, beard and hairline.

brief: Preserve B’s across-bed setting, build the tall row and turn John’s gaze towards the camera. His over-seven-foot canes should read as fine compared with his height. Preserve modest irregularity in the canes and the way the wire is twisted at each joint. Added sky above the original 16:9 framing to show the tips at the 3:2 print aspect.
prompt:
Edit the FIRST photograph, the wide side-on frame B of John in the June allotment, into a finished documentary photograph for his gardening book. B is the photographic plate, not a loose location reference. Keep its viewpoint, cross-row direction, left-to-right orientation, original clear sunlight, existing bed, soil, paths, the adjacent alliums, blue sky, houses and two sheds exactly where seen: the open door of the pale green shed behind John left of centre and the neighbour's brown number 7 shed well to the right. Keep BOTH existing horizontal rows of irregular young bean seedlings in precisely THIS foreground bed. Keep John immediately behind them, same location, ordinary physical size, hand position adjusted naturally, full body, exact blue fleece with brown top and jeans. Simply have him lift his head and look at the camera as in ref 4, naturally relaxed, with the likeness, narrowing lower jaw, short grey beard and proportions in ref 5. Do not zoom towards him. If canvas needs more headroom for cane tops, extend mainly ABOVE frame B, preserve its broadside camera angle, don't convert it into the oblique view in reference D. Output a landscape 3:2 photograph suited to showing the entire finished row, both feet and all tips.
The main change to B: in the same two real lines of beans complete the traditional double row, opposite bamboo poles leaning towards one another ACROSS the bed, each near/far pair crossing high above the central line and tied to a single continuous long horizontal slim ridge. The row runs broadly LEFT TO RIGHT in this camera's view. The two parallel lines of cane feet must be separated by the same real bed width B shows, one line beside the foreground seedlings and one beside those beyond. Use about seven pairs along the bed; hands on one or naturally relaxed with a cane beside John. His face should be in the clear gap between uprights.
Proportions straight from life: these are FULL LENGTH over-seven-foot bamboo garden canes. THIS IS A TALL SPINDLY STRUCTURE. At John's position the ridge is visibly ABOVE the crown of his head when standing fully upright, projecting crossing tips higher still, a clear head or so of scale difference. Keep the same very slim diameter of the EXISTING weathered canes B shows beside his hand: a shaft is slimmer than one finger, only a few pixels wide at entire-frame scale, tip finer again. Do not enlarge the cane diameter, bindings or head to make them legible. The second photograph (D) tells how tall and slender the completed row looks and how the real canes sit under tension; keep B's camera and the main paired structure, the slim longitudinal ridge at the crossings; no added bracing obscuring this broadside teaching view. The natural bamboo is a muted mix of silvery grey, grey-brown and tan from use, gently tapering to the top. Keep individual canes looking like distinct pieces of bamboo: a couple very nearly straight, others slightly bowed in one direction over their full length, a slight departure from straight near an individual node; some lean a little differently. The tips extend uneven amounts above the ridge; the line of crossings and slightly flexed ridge has subtle variation from pair to pair. NO S curves, strongly bowed arches, fat timber dowels, identical plastic-looking poles or perfect repeated triangles.
Third photograph F is a magnification of the REAL fastening, not its size at wide view: short pieces of dark green plastic-coated wire hand-wrapped around the horizontal and crossed poles, a turn or two gripping the bamboo, ends twisted around each other with SHORT bent ends. Each is slightly different: tuck a tail down on one, angle it sideways on another, a double turn and a shorter twist on a third. No bright green rope, crossed bow ties, consistently placed identical knots, decorative bindings or massive green joints. In the full view each is only a small, slightly different dark-green mark. The technique should look tall, light and handmade, like John's film. Keep strong original resemblance to frame B over everything else. No inset, words, letters or overlays.
detail_edit: Local photo retouch of the supplied crop, same framing and registration. Three tips project into the sky at present. Erase only the thin, dark, nearly vertical MIDDLE sliver between the two angled bamboo tips; return that sliver all the way to the joint to the surrounding smooth blue sky. Leave precisely TWO projecting bamboo tips: the shorter light cane leaning upper left and the long tan cane leaning upper right, each continuous to the opposite leg below the ridge. Preserve surrounding sky colour, existing joint location, horizontal cane, green hand-twisted wire, trees and rooftop absolutely registered. No further changes.

checks.confirmed: Both folios preserve the text, trim, image positions and page drawing commands. All rendered changes on page 166 lie inside the bean-row picture. Page 167 is pixel-identical to the preceding proof.
